[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance defines the enterprise architecture approach for building and sustaining a federated ecosystem of AI agents. It establishes the principles, platform constraints, capability grouping method, governance roles, lifecycle model, and risk controls that enterprise architects and domain leads need to design and operate a federated AI agent portfolio that remains governable at scale.
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#business-value]

### Business Value

A governed federated model allows domain teams to innovate locally within enterprise contracts while shared standards keep outputs consistent, auditable, and compliant. Without this architecture, federated delivery typically produces overlapping capabilities, uncontrolled quality drift, unclear ownership, and rising operational burden with low reuse.

[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#target-audience]

- **Primary Audience**: Enterprise architects and solution architects designing the federated AI agent ecosystem
- **Secondary Audience**: Platform Governance Team leads responsible for operating the governance model; High-Tech domain owners setting up capability domains
- **Stakeholders**: Enterprise Copilot Architecture Board; Data and Compliance Owners

[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#business-drivers]

#### Business Drivers

- **Federated delivery demand**: Domain teams across the enterprise want to build AI agents for their own workflow areas. Centralizing all build activity is not viable at this scale; a federated model is required.
- **Governance exposure from low-barrier creation**: The M365 platform makes it easy to create agents. Without a governance architecture, the portfolio grows into an unauditable, overlapping collection of capabilities.
- **Compliance and policy consistency requirements**: Agents that produce outputs for business decisions must meet consistent policy, provenance, and quality standards regardless of which team built them.
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#strategic-alignment]

#### Strategic Alignment

A governed federated model is the operational architecture for the enterprise AI agent program. It enables local innovation within enterprise contracts, supports the talent development objectives of the AI consumer role model, and provides the governance evidence required for enterprise risk management.
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#m365-platform-constraints-to-architect-for]

#### M365 Platform Constraints to Architect For

Enterprise architects must design the governance model to address these platform constraints. Each constraint has an architecture response.

| Platform Constraint | Architecture Response |
|---|---|
| Non-deterministic LLM behavior: identical prompts may produce varied outputs | Enforce output contracts, validation rubrics, and quality thresholds per STD-TEC-AI-003 and STD-TEC-AI-005 |
| Grounding and context variability: response quality depends on available and permissioned context | Define required evidence minimums and degraded-mode behavior per STD-TEC-AI-002 |
| Permission-trimmed data access: users only see data they are authorized to access | Design for role-based evidence expectations; avoid universal data assumptions |
| Prompt fragility and drift: prompt edits can unintentionally change behavior | Versioned canonical prompts, change control, and regression validation per STD-TEC-AI-004 and STD-GOV-AI-004 |
| Connector and source dependency sensitivity: missing or stale sources degrade output quality | Source health checks and explicit degraded-mode output labeling per PTN-TEC-AI-006 |
| Limited shared observability in citizen-built assets | Mandatory telemetry metadata and portfolio-level reporting per STD-TEC-AI-006 |
| Rapid growth pressure: low barrier to creation increases duplicate solutions | Capability registry, overlap analysis, and retirement policy per STD-GOV-AI-005 |
page_texts.17:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#problem-description]

#### Problem Description

In a federated model where many teams create capabilities simultaneously, the ecosystem degrades predictably along five dimensions without architecture controls:
1. Duplicate or overlapping agents that serve semantically equivalent intents
2. Inconsistent quality and output formats between teams
3. Unclear ownership and support boundaries
4. Uncontrolled policy and compliance risk from divergent policy application
5. Rising operational burden with low reuse

[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#principle-1-capability-first-architecture]

#### Principle 1: Capability-First Architecture

**Description:** Group and govern AI agents by stable business capabilities, not by tool availability, data source proximity, or ad hoc prompt inventories.

**Rationale:** Business capabilities are more stable over time than tools or data configurations. Capability-based grouping produces governance boundaries that remain valid as the technology evolves.

**Application:** For every proposed agent, identify the business capability it serves before defining any technical approach. Use the agent grouping method in the Practical Application section to determine whether the capability belongs in an existing group or warrants a new group.
page_texts.22:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#principle-2-federated-delivery-with-centralized-guardrails]

#### Principle 2: Federated Delivery with Centralized Guardrails

**Description:** Central governance defines standards, policy controls, and quality bars. Domain teams own business-specific capability evolution within those controls.

**Rationale:** Fully centralized delivery cannot scale to enterprise volume. Fully decentralized delivery produces governance drift. The federated model captures the benefits of both while accepting the complexity of operating the hub-and-spoke governance structure.

**Application:** Define which decisions are central (standards, policy, cross-domain approvals) and which are local (capability scope, evidence sources, quality targets above the floor). Document this boundary in the governance role definitions. See ADR-GOV-011 for the architectural decision record.
page_texts.23:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#principle-3-reuse-before-new-build]

#### Principle 3: Reuse Before New Build

**Description:** A new agent is approved only when existing capabilities cannot satisfy the need within agreed thresholds.

**Rationale:** In a platform with low creation barriers, the default without this principle is new build. Reuse creates pressure on existing capabilities to remain high-quality and current; new build without reuse pressure produces a portfolio that expands without improving.

**Application:** Every new capability proposal must include an overlap analysis against the portfolio registry before entering Pilot state. If high overlap is confirmed, the team and governance reviewer determine whether the need can be met by extending an existing capability.
page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#principle-4-contract-driven-agent-design]

#### Principle 4: Contract-Driven Agent Design

**Description:** Every agent has a capability contract, intent catalog, evidence map, output contract, and quality rubric before any prompt is authored.

**Rationale:** Agents without explicit contracts produce outputs that cannot be objectively validated, owned, or governed. Contracts are the governance foundation, not supplemental documentation.

**Application:** Follow the Contract-First Agent Pattern (PTN-TEC-AI-009). All four contract artifacts must be complete and reviewed before prompt authoring begins.
page_texts.25:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#principle-5-policy-by-default]

#### Principle 5: Policy by Default

**Description:** Compliance, taxonomy, naming, and provenance controls are mandatory baseline requirements for all capabilities at all lifecycle states.

**Rationale:** Policy-optional models require teams to opt in to compliance. In a federated model, opt-in results in inconsistent application. Mandatory baseline requirements are the only model that scales.

**Application:** Centralize all cross-cutting policy controls in the shared instruction set per the Shared Guardrail Pattern (PTN-TEC-AI-010). Local forks of shared policy are not permitted in Production state.
page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#principle-6-lifecycle-discipline]

#### Principle 6: Lifecycle Discipline

**Description:** Agents move through formal lifecycle states (Proposed, Pilot, Production, Contained, Retired) with explicit entry and exit criteria for each transition.

**Rationale:** Without lifecycle governance, capabilities stay in Production indefinitely regardless of quality degradation, ownership gaps, or portfolio overlap. Lifecycle discipline enables portfolio rationalization and creates the mechanism for evidence-based governance decisions.

**Application:** Every capability must have a defined owner, validation date, and lifecycle state in the portfolio registry. Lifecycle state transitions require change records per STD-GOV-AI-004.
page_texts.28:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#approach-1-hub-and-spoke-deployment-model]

#### Approach 1: Hub-and-Spoke Deployment Model

**Overview:** A central hub publishes mandatory architecture standards and templates, provides shared quality rubrics and taxonomy, and operates the enterprise capability catalog. Business team spokes build and operate domain assets within the hub's standards.

**When to Use:** This is the required deployment model for the enterprise AI agent program. It applies to all domain teams operating under the federated governance model.

**Implementation:** Establish the five governance roles (see Federated Operating Model in the Implementation Framework). Define the team adoption tiers:
- Tier 1: Consumer teams — use approved Production capabilities
- Tier 2: Controlled contributors — extend existing capabilities under review
- Tier 3: Domain maintainers — own lifecycle, quality, and consolidation decisions for a domain

**Benefits:** Hub-and-spoke balances local delivery velocity with enterprise governance consistency. Central standards do not require central build.

**Considerations:** The hub's governance capacity constrains the rate at which domain teams can advance to higher adoption tiers. Governance capacity planning is required.
page_texts.29:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#approach-2-capability-domain-topology]

#### Approach 2: Capability Domain Topology

**Overview:** Organize all agents into a bounded set of capability domains, each with defined boundaries and handoff rules.

**When to Use:** When establishing a new enterprise AI agent program or rationalizing an existing portfolio with unclear domain structure.

**Implementation:** Define capability domains around stable business outcomes. Use the agent grouping criteria to assign each capability to a domain. Define the handoff rules between domains explicitly. Example domain topology from the source architecture guidance:
- Daily orchestration
- Meeting intelligence
- Work prioritization
- Planning and delivery structuring
- Executive and PMO reporting
- Document comparison and change analysis
- Cross-cutting standards and compliance

The domain topology is not fixed — it must be reassessed annually as the portfolio evolves.

**Benefits:** Capability domains provide governance scoping: each domain has an owner, a quality review cadence, and defined boundaries.

**Considerations:** Domain topology decisions made early constrain how the portfolio expands. Over-narrow domain definitions fragment the portfolio; over-broad ones create mega-domains that are difficult to govern.
page_texts.31:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#best-practice-1-define-domain-boundaries-before-the-portfolio-grows]

#### Best Practice 1: Define Domain Boundaries Before the Portfolio Grows

**Description:** Establish the initial capability domain topology and grouping criteria before the portfolio reaches a scale that makes reorganization costly.

**Rationale:** Domain boundaries defined reactively must be imposed on existing capabilities that were built without them. This creates more governance overhead than designing the boundaries before build.

**Implementation:** During the governance architecture setup phase, produce the initial domain topology and register it. Socialize the domain boundaries with all potential domain teams before they begin building.

**Success Indicators:** New capability proposals reference an existing domain at intake. Cross-domain overlaps are detected and resolved before entering Pilot.
page_texts.32:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#best-practice-2-calibrate-alert-thresholds-during-pilot]

#### Best Practice 2: Calibrate Alert Thresholds During Pilot

**Description:** Define metric alert thresholds based on actual Pilot period baseline data, not on estimates made before any operational evidence exists.

**Rationale:** Thresholds set before any operational data tend to be either too sensitive (producing false positives) or too loose (missing real problems). The Pilot period provides the evidence needed for accurate calibration.

**Implementation:** Collect all mandatory metrics per STD-TEC-AI-006 throughout Pilot. At the end of Pilot, set alert thresholds above the observed Pilot baseline. Record the calibration rationale.

**Success Indicators:** Alert threshold breach rate in early Production is consistent with Pilot defect and rework rates. No significant false-positive or false-negative alert events in the first 60 days of Production.
page_texts.34:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#pitfall-1-tool-driven-grouping]

#### Pitfall 1: Tool-Driven Grouping

**Description:** Grouping capabilities based on data source availability or tool access rather than business capability.

**Impact:** Tool-driven groups change scope every time the tool or data access configuration changes. Quality rubrics and output contracts defined for tool-based groups become invalid when the tool changes.

**Prevention:** Apply the seven agent grouping criteria before any technical design. The business capability question must be answered before the tool question.

**Mitigation:** If tool-driven grouping is discovered after build, run the grouping method retroactively. Identify the correct business capability for each existing capability and reorganize the domain topology accordingly.
page_texts.35:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#pitfall-2-governance-drift-from-policy-fork-accumulation]

#### Pitfall 2: Governance Drift from Policy Fork Accumulation

**Description:** Teams make minor local exceptions to shared policy instructions, which accumulate into material divergence from the enterprise policy baseline.

**Impact:** Policy compliance audits find inconsistent policy application across the portfolio. Remediation requires reviewing every capability's prompt library.

**Prevention:** Enforce the local fork prohibition from STD-TEC-AI-004 from the first Production capability. Monthly prompt library audits detect drift early.

**Mitigation:** Identify all local forks in the prompt library. Evaluate each against the current shared instruction set. Consolidate conformant forks; raise non-conformant forks as change requests to the shared instruction set.
page_texts.36:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#pitfall-3-capability-immortality]

#### Pitfall 3: Capability Immortality

**Description:** Capabilities remain in Production indefinitely once launched, with no portfolio hygiene process to retire low-value or high-defect capabilities.

**Impact:** Portfolio support burden increases continuously. Low-quality capabilities continue to shape user expectations. Portfolio discoverability decreases as the number of capabilities increases without corresponding value.

**Prevention:** Establish the rationalization trigger conditions per STD-GOV-AI-005 before the portfolio grows large. Define what "low usage" means quantitatively before the first monthly hygiene review.

**Mitigation:** Run a baseline portfolio assessment per PTN-GOV-AI-009. Produce a rationalization status for each capability that meets a trigger condition. Execute dispositions within a defined timeline.

#### Methodology Overview

The federated AI agent governance model is established in three phases: governance infrastructure setup, initial capability domain deployment, and ongoing portfolio operations. These phases apply to a new program. For an existing program with capabilities already in Production, a separate baseline assessment and remediation is needed before ongoing operations can begin.

[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#phase-1-governance-infrastructure]

#### Phase 1: Governance Infrastructure

**Objectives:** Establish the governance roles, standards, templates, and processes required to operate the federated model.

**Prerequisites:** Enterprise Copilot Architecture Board membership and decision rights defined.

**Key Activities:**

1. Define and document the five governance roles with explicit decision rights and escalation paths
2. Publish the applicable standards (STD-TEC-AI-001 through STD-TEC-AI-008, STD-GOV-AI-004, STD-GOV-AI-005) in force
3. Deploy the portfolio registry with all required data fields
4. Author and review the golden path templates (per PTN-GOV-AI-010)
5. Author and publish the shared instruction set with the initial cross-cutting policy controls
6. Define the emergency change criteria

**Deliverables:**

- Governance role definitions with decision rights matrix
- Standards in force (published and communicated to domain teams)
- Portfolio registry operational and accessible
- Golden path templates available to all builders
- Shared instruction set published and under change control

**Success Criteria:** Every governance role has a named owner. Every builder knows where to find the golden path. The portfolio registry is accessible and supports overlap analysis.
page_texts.47:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#phase-2-initial-domain-deployment]

#### Phase 2: Initial Domain Deployment

**Objectives:** Deploy the initial capability domain topology and advance the first capabilities through the governance lifecycle.

**Prerequisites:** Phase 1 complete. At least one Domain Product Owner active.

**Key Activities:**

1. Define the initial capability domain topology using the agent grouping method
2. Conduct the first governance reviews for capabilities entering Pilot
3. Confirm the golden path process works for the first cohort of builders
4. Promote the first capabilities to Production with compliant telemetry

**Deliverables:**

- Capability domain topology registered with domain boundaries and handoff rules
- First Production capabilities with complete change records, telemetry, and quality rubrics
- Initial baseline metrics established for threshold calibration

**Success Criteria:** At least one capability in Production with full contract artifacts, telemetry, and governance records. Portfolio registry reflects the first cohort of capabilities.

[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#preparation-steps]

#### Preparation Steps

1. **Define the governance role matrix**: document which decisions are made by which role, and which require multi-party approval. The five roles are: Enterprise Copilot Architecture Board, Platform Governance Team, Domain Product Owners, Citizen Builders and Team Maintainers, Data and Compliance Owners.

2. **Produce the initial domain topology**: use the agent grouping criteria (see the Decision Framework below) to organize proposed capabilities into domain groups. Validate each group has a single primary business outcome, a coherent input pattern, a coherent output contract, and a coherent risk profile.
page_texts.51:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#execution-steps]

#### Execution Steps

1. **For each new capability proposal**: run the intake form per PTN-GOV-AI-010; conduct the overlap analysis; assign to a domain; route the capability contract for governance review. Do not begin prompt authoring until all contract artifacts are complete and reviewed.

2. **For each lifecycle state transition**: for promotions (Proposed→Pilot, Pilot→Production), confirm the applicable quality gate criteria from STD-TEC-AI-005 are met and require quality gate sign-off; for non-promotion transitions (Contain, Retire), route through the ownership/lifecycle-change approval tier (domain owner approval); in all cases, submit the change as a change record per STD-GOV-AI-004 and record the approval evidence.
page_texts.52:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#validation-steps]

#### Validation Steps

1. **Monthly**: run the domain hygiene review per STD-GOV-AI-005; evaluate all active capabilities against rationalization trigger conditions; review threshold breach alerts; confirm all Production capabilities have current operational metadata.

2. **Quarterly**: run the enterprise consolidation review; identify cross-domain overlap patterns; assess capabilities with open rationalization reviews; consume the enterprise scorecard.
page_texts.54:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#decision-point-1-should-a-proposed-use-case-be-a-new-capability-or-an-extension-of-an-existing-one]

#### Decision Point 1: Should a proposed use case be a new capability or an extension of an existing one?

**Context:** A team proposes a new capability that may overlap with an existing registered capability.

**Options:** New capability, or extension of an existing capability by adding to its in-scope intent list.

**Criteria:**
- Different business outcome and definition of done → new capability
- Materially different evidence pattern → new capability
- Different output contract and audience → new capability
- Different risk and governance boundary → new capability
- Otherwise → extend the existing capability contract

**Recommendation:** Prefer extension unless at least one of the four differentiation criteria is clearly met. Document the rationale for the choice in the change record or capability contract.
page_texts.55:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#decision-point-2-should-a-capability-be-split-into-two-separate-capabilities]

#### Decision Point 2: Should a capability be split into two separate capabilities?

**Context:** An existing capability has grown beyond a single coherent business outcome, or its defect and rework rate is rising.

**Options:** Keep as one capability, split into two.

**Criteria (split signals from agent grouping guidance):**
- Conflicting output contracts within the same capability
- Conflicting policy boundaries within the same capability
- Incompatible risk profiles within the same capability
- More than the defined maximum recurring intent count for the domain
- Two distinct user populations with different definitions of done

**Recommendation:** Split when two or more split signals are confirmed. Define the two new capability contracts and the handoff boundary before beginning the split execution.
page_texts.57:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#artifact-1-capability-contract]

#### Artifact 1: Capability Contract

**Purpose:** Defines the capability cell boundary, evidence sources, output contract, quality rubric, and ownership.

**Usage:** Required before Pilot promotion per STD-TEC-AI-001. Used as the authoritative reference for all governance reviews.

**Location:** Use the template from the golden path per PTN-GOV-AI-010.
page_texts.58:
[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#artifact-2-architecture-decision-checklist]

#### Artifact 2: Architecture Decision Checklist

**Purpose:** Confirms that all pre-build architecture questions are answered before a capability enters build.

**Usage:** Complete before beginning capability contract authoring for any new proposal. Questions from the source architecture guidance:
1. What business capability is being served?
2. Why can existing capabilities not satisfy this need?
3. What is the capability contract and owner?
4. What evidence is required, optional, and prohibited?
5. What is the output contract and audience?
6. What are the validation criteria and acceptance thresholds?
7. What lifecycle state and review cadence apply?
8. What is the retirement trigger if value is not sustained?

[strategy/guidance/technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-002-enterprise-agent-governance-guidance.md#use-case-1-new-domain-team-establishing-their-first-capability]

#### Use Case 1: New domain team establishing their first capability

**Scenario Description:** A domain team is building their first AI agent capability under the federated model.

**Context:** The team has a clear business use case and domain expertise, but limited familiarity with the enterprise governance process.

**Guidance Application:** Route the team through the golden path per PTN-GOV-AI-010. Starting with the intake form, the team identifies their capability domain, runs the overlap analysis, and completes the contract artifacts in the required sequence before any prompt authoring. The Platform Governance Team provides a designated reviewer for the team's first governance gate.

**Success Factors:** A governance reviewer assigned to the team's first gate; golden path templates available and complete.

#### Use Case 2: Architect rationalizing an existing portfolio

**Scenario Description:** An enterprise architect is asked to rationalize an existing portfolio that grew without formal governance, with multiple overlapping capabilities and unclear ownership.

**Context:** Several capabilities are in Production with no current owners, no validated quality rubrics, and overlapping intent coverage.

**Guidance Application:** Run a baseline portfolio assessment per PTN-GOV-AI-009. Evaluate every capability against the rationalization trigger conditions. Produce a rationalization disposition for each triggered capability. Establish the governance infrastructure that was missing before resuming new capability development.

**Success Factors:** Commitment from the Enterprise Copilot Architecture Board to enforce rationalization decisions; clear communication to domain teams about the new governance requirements.

#### Governance Structure

The federated AI agent governance model uses five roles with defined decision rights:

| Role | Decision Rights | Escalation Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Enterprise Copilot Architecture Board | Standards, risk posture, portfolio guardrails, cross-domain capability approvals, policy change approvals | Final authority for governance exceptions |
| Platform Governance Team | Lifecycle controls, policy baseline operations, quality assurance, capability registry, change governance process | Escalates to Architecture Board for policy and architecture-level decisions |
| Domain Product Owners | Business outcomes, intent catalogs, quality targets within domain, domain-level change approvals | Escalates to Platform Governance Team for cross-domain impacts |
| Citizen Builders and Team Maintainers | Build and improve domain assets within approved contracts and standards | Escalates to Domain Product Owner for scope changes |
| Data and Compliance Owners | Evidence source usage boundaries, policy controls | Participates in cross-domain policy reviews |

#### Risk Assessment

| Risk Category | Risk Description | Mitigation Strategy |
|---|---|---|
| Structural risk | Overlapping capabilities and unclear boundaries | Capability domain topology, overlap analysis at intake, quarterly boundary review per STD-GOV-AI-005 |
| Operational risk | Inconsistent quality and high rework | Quality rubrics, regression checks, threshold-based containment per STD-TEC-AI-005 and STD-TEC-AI-006 |
| Compliance risk | Inconsistent policy application across teams | Centralized shared instruction set per PTN-TEC-AI-010, monthly prompt library audit per STD-TEC-AI-004 |
| Sustainability risk | Owner turnover and unmanaged assets | Ownership metadata requirement, backup owner requirement, lifecycle gates, retirement policy per STD-GOV-AI-005 |

### Maturity Model

| Maturity Level | Description | Characteristics | Next Steps |
|---|---|---|---|
| Level 1: Initial | Federated delivery without governance structure | No portfolio registry; no capability contracts; no change control | Establish governance infrastructure; begin contract authoring for existing capabilities |
| Level 2: Defined | Governance structure established; standards published; registry active | Standards in force; registry populated; some capabilities with contracts | Complete contract authoring for all Production capabilities; begin golden path onboarding |
| Level 3: Governed | All Production capabilities have contracts, telemetry, and change records | Portfolio registry current; monthly hygiene reviews running; change gateway in use | Begin quarterly consolidation reviews; calibrate metric thresholds from Pilot baselines |
| Level 4: Optimizing | Telemetry actively drives governance decisions | Scorecard-driven reviews; rationalization producing measurable portfolio improvement | Continuous improvement of governance cadence; advanced telemetry-to-governance feedback |
